extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy; legislators and anyone seeking practical ethical guidance
extracted.subtask_description: A practical account of moral virtue focused on how virtues are formed, what their nature is, how to find the mean between excess and defect, and how to judge voluntariness of actions. Intended as guidance for becoming virtuous and for legislators assigning praise and blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtues acquired by habituation
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues are formed by repeatedly doing the relevant actions: 'we get the faculties first and perform the acts of working afterwards' (senses are natural), but 'the Virtues we get by first performing single acts of working' — e.g. men become builders by building, harp-players by playing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises practice and repeated performance rather than mere theoretical knowledge; lawgivers aim to make citizens good by habituation. Examples and anti-patterns: unlike natural faculties, virtues require doing (not merely learning) and cannot be gained by talk alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits are produced or destroyed by the same circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Virtue is either produced or destroyed from and by the very same circumstances that form it: e.g., by playing the harp both good and bad harp-players are formed; by building well men become good builders, by building badly bad ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies that formation and corruption of character share causes; instructor/education matters because without proper habituation people would not become good or bad in their arts/virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act in accordance with Right Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: A general maxiom: 'we are to act in accordance with Right Reason' — the standard by which moral action should be judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text takes this as a starting assumption to be elaborated later; practical judgement must combine right reason with context-sensitive application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral action lacks exactness; judge by particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: All that can be said about moral action must be said 'in outline, as it were, and not exactly' because particular cases do not fall under any fixed art or system of rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral reasoning must leave room for individual judgment in specific situations (like medicine or navigation). Do not expect universal exact prescriptions; aim for principles and prudential judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtues spoiled by excess and defect; preserved by the mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits of perfected Self-Mastery and Courage (and other virtues) are spoiled by excess and defect and preserved by the mean state: e.g., fearing all things makes a coward, fearing nothing makes one rash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate character traits by locating them relative to two vices (excess and defect) and identifying the mean as the virtuous state. Use examples (food, training) to illustrate how excess/defect harm good states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of formation: pleasure or pain following acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The formation of virtuous habits is tested by the pleasure or pain that follows actions: 'he is perfected in Self-Mastery who not only abstains but is glad to do so; he is brave who stands up against danger either with positive pleasure or at least without any pain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure internal responses as indicators of genuine habituation. Abstaining with regret indicates absence of true self-mastery; enduring danger with pain is not full courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue's object-matter is pleasures and pains
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Virtue has for its object-matter pleasures and pains, because pleasure often motivates bad action and pain deters right action; virtues aim to manage pleasure and pain rightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education and law should train appropriate responses to pleasure/pain. Punishments and remedies work via pleasures/pains; correct 'impressions' of pleasure/pain are crucial for moral action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue is a State (disposition), not a Feeling or Capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues belong to the class of States — dispositions regarding feelings and actions — rather than mere Feelings (anger, fear) or Capacities (ability to feel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States involve stable dispositions, are subject to praise/blame, and require moral choice. This distinguishes virtuous possession from merely having feelings or natural capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue is a mean relative to us, determined by reason and practical wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is 'a state apt to exercise deliberate choice, being in the relative mean, determined by reason, and as the man of practical wisdom would determine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mean is not an absolute arithmetic midpoint but the right amount relative to the agent and situation; practical wisdom (phronesis) is required to determine it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative (not absolute) mean — tailored to the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes absolute mean (arithmetical) from the mean relatively to ourselves — what is neither too much nor too little for the particular individual (e.g., Milo vs a novice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, skill and judgement adapt requirements to the agent's situation and capacities; avoid rigid, one-size-fits-all standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some actions/feelings are intrinsically bad and admit no mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain feelings and actions (e.g., malevolence, shamelessness, envy; adultery, theft, homicide) are bad in themselves and do not admit a mean between excess and defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to find a middle ground for intrinsically wrongful acts — any instance is blameworthy. These are categorical prohibitions rather than temperance-regulated matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific virtues as means (catalogue with excess/defect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of the mean to particular domains (summary): I. Courage (mean) between cowardice (defect) and rashness (excess). II. Self-Mastery (mean) between insensibility (defect) and loss of self-control (excess). III. Liberality (mean) between stinginess (defect) and prodigality (excess). IV. Munificence and its excesses/defects. V. Greatness of Soul (mean) between littleness and χαυνότης (excess). VI. Ambition/unambitious (relating to small honours). VII. Meekness (mean) between passionateness (excess) and angerlessness (defect). Plus: Truthfulness (vs braggadocio/reserve), Easy-pleasantry (vs buffoonery/clownishness), Friendliness (vs complaisance/flattery/quarrelsomeness), Shamefacedness, Indignation against successful vice (mean between envy and malevolence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use domain-specific names for mean and extremes when evaluating actions and character. The listing is an 'outline and summary' to be refined later; names may vary with scale (e.g., liberality vs munificence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relational opposition of extremes and perspectival judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: The extremes are opposed to one another and to the mean; the mean may look like an extreme when compared to the opposite extreme (e.g., the brave man appears rash to the coward and cowardly to the rash).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of virtue are perspectival; critics from extreme dispositions may mislabel the mean. Recognise this when evaluating character across different observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which extreme is 'more contrary' matters for corrective strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the two extremes, one will often be more contrary to the mean than the other (e.g., cowardice is more contrary to courage than rashness is; excess of pleasure is more contrary to self-mastery than insensibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for the mean, it is safer to guard against the extreme that is more contrary; take the lesser of evils and steer away from the most dangerous extreme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical precautions for attaining the mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical advice: identify which extreme is more contrary, take the least evil as safest, consider one's natural bias (especially toward pleasure), deliberately move away from one's biased side (like straightening bent timber), and guard carefully against pleasure because we are not impartial judges of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use force-of-habit and intentional corrective motion (sometimes overshooting to the opposite side) to arrive at the mean; the Moral Sense helps judge borderline deviations in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary vs involuntary actions (two kinds of involuntary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Involuntary actions are of two kinds: those done under compulsion (origination external to the agent, agent contributes nothing) and those done by reason of ignorance; voluntary actions originate in the agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish cases: actions done under threat may be 'mixed' but are often like voluntary actions because origination of movement rests with the agent at the time. The status (voluntary/involuntary) determines praise, blame, and legal/moral treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and test of compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: An action is properly compulsory 'when the origination is external to the agent, being such that in it the agent contributes nothing' (e.g., being carried by the wind or coerced by men with power over you).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the criterion for excusing responsibility: if the agent contributes nothing to the action's origination, it is compulsory and typically involuntary; if the agent's limbs originate motion, it is voluntary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance as source of involuntary actions (with remorse condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions done through ignorance are not automatically involuntary; only those attended by pain and remorse (the agent is 'annoyed at his own action') qualify as involuntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the agent's subsequent feelings: lack of remorse suggests the act was not involuntary in the moral sense; remorse and pain make ignorance excusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntariness judged at the time of action
rubrics_metrics.description: We should denominate an action voluntary or involuntary 'at the time of doing it' — if the origination rests with the agent at that time, it counts as voluntary even if we would not choose it in abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixed cases (e.g., throwing goods overboard in a storm) are voluntary in context because the agent's choice at the moment makes the action preferable given circumstances; moral assessment should consider situational choice-worthiness.
